publication.title: Affective Graphs: The Visual Appeal of Linked Data

source_reading.scope: full_report

adjudication.basis: Affective Graphs combines interactive schema/instance statistics and visual SPARQL construction over RDF/Linked Data, evaluated in two distinct human study designs.

codes.notes: Integration with multi-result-view dashboard is future work, distinct from current graph/query/context panels.

studies.design: Screenshot/layout aesthetic metrics
limitations: Manual screenshot-region annotation, not proof of usability superiority.

studies.design: Comparative user study
tasks: Five Mooney-geography fact-finding queries of varying complexity
comparators: Semantic Crystal, KSearch, Ginseng, NLPReduce; randomised system order
studies.results: Affective Graphs combined SUS 60.0 versus Semantic Crystal 55, KSearch 41.25, Ginseng 40 and NLPReduce 40; NLPReduce had lowest input time, Affective Graphs/Semantic Crystal longer. Affective Graphs among fewest attempts.
limitations: Fact-finding benchmark; different query mechanisms and result displays. Do not claim overall superiority or an isolated aesthetics effect.

studies.design: Repeated-session learnability study
tasks: Four fact-finding task types each session and exploratory tasks in first and third; Semantic Web Dog Food data / USEWOD logs
comparators: Same tool over three one-hour sessions on consecutive days; no separate control
studies.results: Mean input time 106.48 to 72.72 to 66.845 seconds; SUS 76.25 to 82.5 to 81.25. Complex-task attempts median 2 to 2.5 to 3.5; exploratory attempts 3.5 to 5.
limitations: Training and repeated use; participant overlap with comparative study not established. Do not pool samples or causally attribute learning to aesthetics.

descriptions.interaction: Incremental class/pie-section browsing, relation inspection, concept/property search, drag/reposition and context-menu query building with typed filters, OR/negation, result selection/sorting and query preview/edit.
descriptions.guidance: Hierarchy and instance counts in pie nodes, contextual domain/range property panel, highlighting of selected query terms, typed constraints and formal SPARQL access for advanced users. Context panel discoverability and hover burden remained problems.
descriptions.visualisation: Pie-chart concept nodes, distinct hierarchical/data/object edges, Bézier relations, force-directed layout active initially for five seconds then stable; table results. Dashboard/multiple-result-view integration is future work.
descriptions.backend: HTML/JavaScript/Processing.js/CSS/jQuery UI frontend, PHP/ARC2 SPARQL backend with response cache; public endpoints and local Virtuoso in experiments.

studies.response_note: Participants were randomly assigned to interface-order Groups A and B. Group A used the conversational interface for Scenario 1, followed by the graphical interface for Scenario 2; Group B used the graphical interface for Scenario 1, followed by the conversational interface for Scenario 2. Each participant used both interfaces on different scenarios. The described scenario order is fixed (Scenario 1, then Scenario 2). Random assignment concerns the interface-order groups, not randomized scenario order. See primary report Section 4.2, PDF pages 6–7.
studies.design: Counterbalanced two-group crossover; each participant uses both interfaces for different scenarios
comparators: Graphical interface with traditional text search
studies.results: SUS scenario1: conversational76.00(18.94), graphical77.25(15.28); scenario2: conversational76.63(16.63), graphical65.25(23.91). Readability/usefulness/satisfaction ratings generally favor conversation.
limitations: Descriptive rating analysis without reported significance/effect-size test. No objective retrieval/task-time gain established. Main method says approximately10minutes; appendix scenarios specify up to8minutes. Interface assignment/order is counterbalanced between groups; the described scenario order is fixed (Scenario 1 then Scenario 2), and each person sees a given scenario with only one interface.

report_level_evaluation.design: Three distinct evaluations: offline research-topic classification; abstract-sentence classification with qualitative manual inspection of comparisons; and a two-group counterbalanced human comparison. For the human study participants were randomly assigned to Groups A/B with similar demographic distributions. Group A used conversational Scenario 1 then graphical Scenario 2; Group B used graphical Scenario 1 then conversational Scenario 2. Each person used both interfaces on different scenarios; scenario order was fixed in the described sequence.
report_level_evaluation.participants: Human study: 40 recruited participants, Group A n=20 and Group B n=20; Table 3 reports 40 overall participants. Recruited through university courses/social networks; basic technical knowledge and English proficiency, interest in NLP, target non-experts. Ages 20–29, mean 25.03; 14 female and 26 male. Separate component samples: 1,601 synthetic training questions and 364 test questions for topic classification; 500 computer-science abstracts / 3,287 labelled sentences for SciBERT. Two researchers manually assessed generated comparisons. Outcome-specific analytic sample sizes and attrition/completion counts are not separately reported.
report_level_evaluation.tasks: Human exploratory search: find publications on (1) NLP analysis of mental-health/emotion expressions on social media during COVID-19, and (2) automatic generation of multiple-choice exams for a Python programming course. Main method allows approximately 10 minutes per interface; Appendix Table 2 says up to 8 minutes and encourages thinking aloud. Component tasks classify search goals into NLP topics and abstract sentences into rhetorical categories; these are separate from human retrieval tasks.
report_level_evaluation.comparators: Human study compares the conversational scholarly-search interface with the ACL Anthology graphical interface using traditional text search. Topic classification compares SPECTER2-based vector similarity, GPT-3.5-Turbo prompting and a SetFit classifier. Abstract-sentence classification reports a comparison with the prior Gonçalves et al. model; manual comparison-summary assessment is qualitative.
report_level_evaluation.measures: Human study: System Usability Scale (SUS; 0–100), five-point ratings of perceived readability, correctness, usefulness, generated-comparison quality and overall satisfaction, plus two free-text feedback fields. Topic classification: accuracy and macro F1; abstract-sentence classification: reported F1. Human perceived correctness is not an objective retrieval-accuracy score.
report_level_evaluation.results: Human Table 1: SUS conversational/graphical mean (SD) = 76.00 (18.94)/77.25 (15.28) for Scenario 1 and 76.63 (16.63)/65.25 (23.91) for Scenario 2. Readability, perceived correctness, usefulness and satisfaction means favor the conversational interface in both scenarios; summary quality was rated only for the conversational interface. Descriptive ratings and qualitative feedback are reported without an inferential significance or effect-size test. Separate topic-classifier macro F1: vector search below 0.50, prompting near 0.75, SetFit 0.95. Separate SciBERT abstract-sentence F1: 75.39% versus 74.60% in the cited prior model.
report_level_evaluation.limitations: The sample is narrow (40 participants aged 20–29, university/social-network recruitment) and tasks are two predefined scholarly-NLP scenarios. Each participant uses a given scenario with one interface only; interface assignment/order is counterbalanced while described scenario order stays Scenario 1 then Scenario 2. No outcome-specific analytic N, attrition, objective human retrieval-accuracy score, task-time improvement, inferential significance test, confidence interval or standardized effect size is reported. Preserve the approximately-10-minute versus up-to-8-minute timing inconsistency. Reported interaction problems include difficulty learning the three-phase flow, unclear buttons versus free text, and backtracking. Component scores concern synthetic topic questions / abstract-sentence classification, not human search effectiveness.

source_reading.scope: Abstract, annotation configuration, complete demo workflow (§2), related-work comparison and final functionality list.

report_level_evaluation.design: Counterbalanced within-subjects remote comparison with a production baseline; separate offline approximation experiment
report_level_evaluation.participants: user study n: 15; interaction logs n: 10; interview n: 10; background: Graduate students in computing-related fields;4 active Semantic Scholar users and11 trained to curate feeds at least one week before the study; formative pilots: n: 17; population: Semantic Scholar designers/researchers; n: 13; population: Current Semantic Scholar users; offline data: 346 real feeds,30 authors per feed,20% test split
report_level_evaluation.tasks: Two short literature-review tasks using different research feeds: select5 new papers and5 new authors in each condition; inspect multiple lenses afterwards
report_level_evaluation.comparators: Semantic Scholar without FeedLens features; offline summary embeddings compared with exhaustive per-paper scoring and mean-count baseline
report_level_evaluation.measures: NASA-TLX, SUS, system logs, task duration, relevance/diversity/novelty/obviousness of selected items, subjective item ratings, feature usefulness and thematic interviews; offline RMSE/count approximation and speedup
report_level_evaluation.results: FeedLens SUS84(SD8.6) vs77.3(SD12.5), p<.01; cognitive-load ratings2.4(SD1) vs3.3(SD1.3) on1–5 scale. report_level_evaluation.design: Offline benchmark retrieval evaluation and model ablation; separate single-thread runtime experiment
report_level_evaluation.tasks: Entity-list completion from1–5 relevant example entities; INEX2007 used for model analysis, INEX2008,SemSearch2011,QALD3,QALD4 for comparisons
report_level_evaluation.comparators: Random walk with restart, Bron et al. hybrid textual/structural entity-search method, random ranking and QBEES variants
report_level_evaluation.measures: MAP,nDCG,precision,recall,MRR at10/100,ranking length; runtime components and total variant runtime over200 queries repeated3times
report_level_evaluation.results: Stronger variants outperform competing retrieval models for at least2 examples on INEX2008/SemSearch in most settings, with documented exceptions;QALD gains are larger because ground-truth SPARQL star patterns align with aspect structure. Share-threshold+one-step relaxation improves quality/runtime tradeoff. Cold-cache mean components: entity-set retrieval2.22s,candidate construction.12s,maximal aspect computation.06s,ranking/selection.32s. No user-study outcomes are reported.; limits: Only YAGO2 tested; queries/relevance sets change with example count and must not be compared across sizes as matched queries. Entity mapping removes unmappable relevant answers. Benchmarks structurally favor the aspect model, especially QALD. Baseline implementations are not optimized and random-walk runtime was not measured in the same setup; runtime excludes one-time initialization. Iterative navigation is future/separate work.

studies.design: 100randomsets each of2/3/4/5 nodes,60ssearch budgets from10,000degree-weighted candidate nodes
studies.results: 99,609,308 nodes/715,906,922 edges indexed in4.8h/26.9GB. Degree-expansion bound improves medianfound edges/min from24–194to34–1,009and reduces median query memory from7GBto100MB.
limitations: Workload/path discovery rate is not arbitrary-query latency guarantee; heuristics alter explored paths.

descriptions.interaction: Select two or more entities with autocomplete; stream connecting paths into a force-directed graph; click intermediate nodes to highlight their paths; drag nodes and filter path length or intermediate degree.
descriptions.guidance: ["Entity autocomplete", "Explanatory connecting subgraphs", "Progressive path arrivals and selected-node highlighting"]
descriptions.visualisation: ["Directed labelled node-link topical graph", "Entity labels/images", "Numeric pathfilter sliders"]
